wa_storm_king_southwest_scramble.name: The shared Goode approach to 7,400 ft, then the talus cirque and the right-most notch
camps: Rib camp below Storm King/Goode basin
Five Mile Camp, Park Creek trail
wa_storm_king_southwest_scramble.notes:
Storm King sits at the head of Thunder Creek and is one of the range's most remote summits — a three-day car-to-car trip is the norm, and three separate trailhead approaches converge on the same high basin below Goode's south side.

The most common is Thunder Creek: from Colonial Creek Campground on SR-20, the Thunder Creek trail roughly 13 miles with little gain to the McAllister Creek confluence, past Junction, Skagit Queen and Thunder Basin camps, then the Park Creek Pass trail junction and the switchbacks to Park Creek Pass. Alternatives are McAlester Pass and Rainbow Creek from SR-20, or a boat or shuttle to Stehekin and High Bridge Camp then the Park Creek trail from the south. From Stehekin the boot path starts on the north side of a large whitish-rock washout about two miles above the Two Mile camp, near 4,100 ft, five minutes further into the woods.

Every approach joins that trail: from Thunder Creek, cross Park Creek Pass and descend its south side to the washout. Leave the trail at the small cairn, climb the burned ridge beside the washout ravine, trend climber's left through heather and game trails, and follow cairns above about 6,500 ft to the basin below Goode at about 7,400 ft. From there, traverse snow and talus, favouring climber's left, roughly a mile to the cirque below Storm King's east and west towers. A rib camp around 7,450 ft with nearby water is the usual base.

From the cirque, a long and very loose talus and scree slope leads up toward the southwest gully system. Helmet on and space out — that slope is the approach's main hazard.
wa_storm_king_southwest_scramble.season: Late July through September; snow often lingers in the basin above about 7,400 ft into early August, so carry an axe and consider crampons even for a nominally dry climb
hazards: Very loose talus and scree slope below the summit gully, with rockfall onto parties below
Lingering snow and hard patches on the basin traverse into early August
Exposed class 4 ledge traverse below the summit with real fall consequences
Aging in-situ slings at the crux that need backing up before use
Easy to drift off-line in poor visibility; the route is indistinguishable from the neighbouring peak's below 7,400 ft
Extreme remoteness, assume multi-day evacuation for a serious injury
wa_storm_king_southwest_scramble.baseFinding:
The most important thing to know about this approach is that below 7,400 ft it is indistinguishable from Goode Mountain's. The same trail, the same basin, the same cairned climber's path. A party in fog below that elevation cannot tell from the ground which peak's route it is on. The split happens above it, where this route trends toward the towers while Goode's continue toward the glacier or Black Tooth Notch.

The counting test is the notch, and the word is right-most. There are several notches in the summit rocks; the route crosses at the right-most one. Most of the way up to it is loose scree and talus, which is what makes the notch worth confirming rather than guessing.

Cross to the north side of that notch and the ground changes character completely: a fun ledge traverse on the backside of the tower, roughly 70 ft, with two or three class 4 moves and full exposure. If you have not crossed to the north side, you have not found the ledge traverse, and there is no version of this route that goes up the front.

Confirm on the ledge: it includes a squeeze under a slight overhang, and there are in-situ slings at the crux left by earlier parties. A squeeze move plus old tat is the strongest positive confirmation on the climb — though the tat is aging and is not to be trusted with body weight without backup.

The last move is a choice, not a crux: a 15-ft solid class 4 face crack, or a wrap around its left side on class 3 blocks. Both reach the register and the rappel slings.

And know which top you want: two 8,520-ft-plus points sit east of a triangulated 8,515 ft subsummit, and the easternmost is the true high point.

wa_storm_king_southwest_scramble.name: Stehekin and the Park Creek trail

bivy.name: Rib camp below Storm King/Goode basin
bivy.notes: Flat, grassy camp on a small NE/SW-trending rib just south of Storm King, with a nearby water source. It is reached by a mostly level traverse from the basin below Goode.

bivy.name: Five Mile Camp, Park Creek trail
bivy.notes: The eastern counterpart to Thunder Basin: the last practical night before crossing Park Creek Pass from the Stehekin side, and the staging point for Buckner and Booker approached from the east. The trail above climbs through hanging meadows to the pass with good views of Goode, Buckner and Booker on the way. Coming in from Stehekin turns a very long one-way walk into a shorter approach than the roughly nineteen miles from Colonial Creek, at the cost of a lake crossing and road transport. Which side is faster depends entirely on whether the shuttle is running to the upper valley that season.
bivy.water: Park Creek is immediately adjacent and reliable.
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit required, covering Lake Chelan National Recreation Area as well as the park proper. Permits for an approach started from Stehekin still come through the same park system. Plan around Lake Chelan boat and shuttle schedules, since a missed connection can put you a day off your permitted itinerary.
bivy.capacity: Creekside stock camp on the Park Creek trail. Small; the neighbouring Two Mile camp downvalley was reduced to a single site by past flooding, so do not count on it as overflow.

wa_storm_king_southwest_scramble.notes: Take the boat up the lake to Stehekin and the shuttle to High Bridge, then walk up the valley past Bridge Creek to the Park Creek trail and climb it past Two Mile Camp. About a mile before Five Mile Camp, look for cairns marking a class 2-3 climbers' path up to the basin below Goode at about 7,400 ft. The least climbing of the three ways if the boat and shuttle schedule suits.
hazards: Seasonal washouts and stream crossings on the Park Creek trail approach
Lake crossing and shuttle schedule: a missed connection puts you a day behind
Off-trail climbers' path up a burned ridge beside a washout, easy to miss at the cairn
Lingering snow on the basin traverse into early August
Very loose talus and scree slope below the summit gully, rockfall onto parties below
Exposed class 4 ledge traverse below the summit
Extreme remoteness, assume multi-day evacuation

wa_storm_king_southwest_scramble.name: Cascade Pass and the upper Stehekin valley

bivy.name: Rib camp below Storm King/Goode basin
bivy.notes: Flat, grassy camp on a small NE/SW-trending rib just south of Storm King, with a nearby water source. It is reached by a mostly level traverse from the basin below Goode.

wa_storm_king_southwest_scramble.notes: A drive-to start from the west side when the boat is impractical. Cross Cascade Pass and descend into the Stehekin valley, follow it down to the Park Creek trail, then climb Park Creek to the same cairned climbers' path up to the basin below Goode.
hazards: Long approach over Cascade Pass and down the upper Stehekin valley before the Park Creek trail
Seasonal washouts and stream crossings on the Park Creek trail
Off-trail climbers' path up a burned ridge beside a washout, easy to miss at the cairn
Lingering snow on the basin traverse into early August
Very loose talus and scree slope below the summit gully, rockfall onto parties below
Exposed class 4 ledge traverse below the summit
Extreme remoteness, assume multi-day evacuation

wa_summit_chief_mountain_south_route.name: Pete Lake and the PCT switchbacks to the Vista Lakes tarns
wa_summit_chief_mountain_south_route.notes:
Walk the Pete Lake trail #1323 up the Cooper River to a fork at about 3,120 ft, roughly five miles in. Turn right, continue about six tenths of a mile, and turn right again onto the Pacific Crest Trail at about 3,220 ft. Follow the PCT four and a half miles up a long series of switchbacks to about 5,500 ft.

The Vista Lakes tarns lie east of the trail at that height and hold the good bivy sites. Summit Chief is about two more miles from there. Reported times from the car to the upper lake run to most of a day with overnight loads, and every published account treats this as a two- or three-day trip.

This is also the last reliable water. The ground above is reported bone dry until you come back down to the lakes.

From camp, leave the PCT and traverse cross-country toward Summit Chief Pass, then follow the ridge north-west staying below the cliffs and gendarmes, into the upper basin south-east of the main summit. One party's hindsight on this traverse is worth having: they should have dropped to about 6,000 ft and taken the scree instead of holding height across steep sloping slabs.
wa_summit_chief_mountain_south_route.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, but see the moat note — the gate at 7,000 ft can shut by mid-July, earlier in a thin snow year
hazards: A moat around 7,000 ft that can close the route outright after mid-July
Icy gully beyond the notch in the morning — crampons are worth carrying for it
Steep dirt and very loose rock on the final five hundred feet
Rockfall from parties above on the hardpan and talus below the notch
No water at all above the Vista Lakes
Sloping slabs on the traverse from camp, avoidable by dropping to the scree around 6,000 ft
wa_summit_chief_mountain_south_route.baseFinding:
There is a specific chain of features here and it ends at a piece of ground that is unmistakable once you know to look for it.

From the upper basin, find a small notch in the skyline ridge to the west. To reach it, head north-west toward a minor rock ridge that runs west-south-west to east-north-east across the base of the summit. That minor ridge is the base of the climb — arriving at it is arriving.

Gain it by the snow in the gap at its right, lower end, then walk along the top of the ridge to the notch at its west end. On the far side of the notch is a steep gully, usually icy in the morning, and beyond that a loose-rock gully; the exit is the gully on the right just below the summit.

Negative marker, learned the hard way and independently corroborated: from the snowfield below the south-east face, the first and left-most snow finger leading to the south ridge is a dead end. It runs into a deep notch and the party that took it had to retreat. Go instead to the upper right corner of the snowfield, exit onto steep dirt and scree, and pick up a left-slanting ramp to a higher notch. Two separate accounts arrive at the same instruction from opposite directions.

The moat is the gate and it has a date on it. Where the mountain rises in earnest at about 7,000 ft a moat forms, and it may be impassable after mid-July, perhaps earlier in a low-snow year. If it stops you, there may be Class 3 rock in the middle of the basin as an alternative, but plan the trip around the calendar rather than hoping.

Do not trust a single photograph for the crossing point on the south ridge; parties report the pictures circulating online do not match the ground.

The top five hundred feet is steep dirt and thoroughly untrustworthy rock — one climber said it had earned honorary Olympic Mountains status. That looseness is normal for this summit and is not a sign you have wandered onto harder ground.

wa_summit_chief_mountain_south_route.name: Lemah Meadow shortcut, cutting the PCT switchbacks
wa_summit_chief_mountain_south_route.notes: A recorded variant that saves about three miles. After gaining roughly a thousand feet on the tight PCT switchbacks, leave the trail at the corner around 4,000 ft and head north, climbing about six hundred feet to the crest. The party who did it found plenty of windfall and pockets of vine maple, and called it irritating rather than difficult. It is a single-source variant, so treat the line as a hint rather than a route.
wa_summit_chief_mountain_south_route.season: Same window; the bypass is brushier and is a trade of distance for thrashing
hazards: Windfall and vine maple on the bypass
No tread and no cairns
Same moat and loose-rock hazards above
wa_summit_chief_mountain_south_route.baseFinding:
The shortcut rejoins the standard line on the crest above and does not change where the climbing starts. Everything from the upper basin onward is as for the standard approach: the skyline notch to the west, the minor rock ridge running west-south-west across the base of the summit, the snow gap at its lower right end, and the moat around 7,000 ft as the real gate.

What you lose by taking it is the view of the peak that the PCT switchbacks give you on the way up, so identify the minor ridge and the notch from the basin rather than expecting to have already picked them out.

wa_swiss_peak_standard_route.name: The northern line: Access Creek and Luna Col, then the high traverse over Luna, East Fury and West Fury to the Swiss-Fury saddle
camps: Luna Col bivy, Luna cross-country zone
wa_swiss_peak_standard_route.notes:
From the Ross Dam Trailhead at milepost 134 on WA-20, about a mile of trail and service road drops to Ross Lake, crossed by the resort water taxi or by paddling or walking round. Pick up the Big Beaver Trail north along the lake and follow it roughly 10 miles to Luna Camp, then about 1.5 miles further to the Access Creek drainage.

Leave the trail and climb the brushy, moderately steep Access Creek valley, staying on its north side, to the open basin east of Luna Peak at about 4,300 ft. This is described as the easiest and least brushy approach on the east side of the Pickets. From there, gain Access Col and traverse cross-country and glaciated terrain over Luna Peak, East Fury and West Fury to reach the Swiss-Fury saddle.
hazards: Glacier or snowfield crossing near West Fury toward the saddle carries crevasse and moat hazard
Traverse over Luna, East Fury and West Fury is required just to reach the saddle
Steep brushy off-trail travel in the Access Creek drainage
Extreme remoteness, no quick bailout; any injury means multi-day self-rescue
Exposed knife-edge summit ridge with a roughly 2,000 ft drop into Luna Cirque
Loose rock on some approach pinnacles
wa_swiss_peak_standard_route.baseFinding: The base is a saddle between two named summits and you reach it by having crossed both summits of Fury. That is a hard test to fail and a hard one to pass: there is no way to arrive at the Swiss-Fury saddle by this line without having traversed West Fury, so if you have not climbed Fury, you are not there. Arrival: a saddle is the low point between two rises. From it, this route climbs the southwest face, and the descent runs back down near the northwest ridge toward the same saddle. If the ground above you steepens into a face rather than a ridge, that is the route. Nothing marks the foot of the southwest face; what you navigate by is the saddle and the ridge. Do not expect a cairn, a gully or a flake to confirm you; expect the shape of the col. What going too far looks like: continuing northwest along the crest past Swiss takes you toward the ground the Northern Pickets traverse uses, with no easier way down on that side.

wa_swiss_peak_standard_route.name: The southern line: Bacon Creek Road, Porkbelly and Mystery Ridges, Jasper Pass and Crowder's northeast ridge to Pickell Pass

approachLogistics.trailhead: Bacon Creek Road (off SR-20 near Marblemount)

wa_swiss_peak_standard_route.notes:
The alternate, and the shorter of the two in spirit if not in effort. It reaches Swiss from the south via Bacon Creek Road, Porkbelly Ridge, Mystery Ridge, Jasper Pass, Pioneer Ridge and Mount Crowder's northeast ridge, down to a camp at Pickell Pass.

This line is off-trail for most of its length, so treat the ridge sequence as the route rather than any particular tread.
hazards: Long off-trail ridge sequence over Porkbelly, Mystery and Pioneer ridges and Crowder's northeast ridge with no tread
Steep, brushy, sometimes cliffy off-trail terrain
No independent descent; leaving the range means a long off-trail drainage exit
Class 3 south side above Pickell Pass, downclimbed on return
Exposed knife-edge summit ridge with a roughly 2,000 ft drop into Luna Cirque
Extreme remoteness, any injury means multi-day self-rescue
wa_swiss_peak_standard_route.baseFinding:
From Pickell Pass the south side of Swiss is climbed directly, and the test is that you are going up rather than along. Camp is a heather bench at the pass; the climbing starts on the class 3 south side immediately above it. Parties on this line downclimb the same class 3 south side back to the bench, so the ascent and descent are the same ground, and a party that has to traverse to find its line has left the route.

How to know you are at Pickell Pass rather than another saddle on the same ridge system: it is reached by descending Mount Crowder's northeast ridge. The last named summit before the pass is Crowder. If you have not been on Crowder, you have not arrived by this line.

Why this side may be the better choice, as a planning fact rather than a landmark: the northern line requires traversing Luna, East Fury and West Fury. This one does not require crossing Fury at all. The cost is a long ridge sequence with no trail and no bailout.

wa_switchback_mountain_scramble.name: Foggy Dew Creek and Merchants Basin to Cooney Lake
wa_switchback_mountain_scramble.notes: Most parties backpack in and camp at one of the lakes rather than push the whole eighteen to twenty mile round trip in a day. From the Foggy Dew road end the trail climbs the North Fork past a two-tiered cascade — the last easy water before the country opens — and tops out of the timber into a wildflower basin below the ridge, where a spur trail branches toward the lake. An alternative comes in on the Crater Creek and Eagle Lake trail, taking a signed cutoff south past a second set of lakes to reach the same lake basin. Above the lake the ground is dry, so fill there. Larches turn gold around the basin in late September, which is a fine but colder window with a real chance of early snow icing the summit blocks.
wa_switchback_mountain_scramble.season: Mid-July to early October; larch Sep
hazards: Lightning exposure on an open ridge and summit with nowhere to shelter
Loose rock and talus on the southeast ridge
Long, mostly waterless final push above Cooney Lake
Off-trail route-finding from the pass to the summit
Iced summit blocks in shoulder season
Mosquitoes in the lake basins through mid-July
wa_switchback_mountain_scramble.baseFinding: From the lake the trail keeps climbing for roughly another mile, crossing a saddle at about 7,900 ft on the peak's southeast side, and then runs into the broad southeast ridge of the mountain. The point where the tread meets that crest is the base — everything to there is walking on a path, and everything above it is off it. The ridge itself is easy and broad, so the confirmation is the last few hundred feet rather than the first: the crest steepens into a field of large, mostly stable blocks that wants hands only occasionally, with a few more exposed steps possible right at the top. The neighbour to watch for is the similar summit under a mile north along the same crest, which is a comparable height, a comparable walk and shares a lake name with this one in places — parties do link the two, but if you have walked north along easy open ridge for the better part of a mile you are on the other peak.

wa_switchback_mountain_scramble.name: Crater Creek and the Eagle Lakes side

bivy.name: Upper Eagle Lake and Horsehead Pass
bivy.notes: The hub of the southern Sawtooth and the practical base for Switchback Mountain, with Hoodoo and Raven Ridge also within reach along the crest. Access is the Gold Creek side, not the Twisp River: turn off the highway onto the North Fork Gold Creek road, then a signed spur for several miles to the Eagle Lakes trailhead at about 4,760 ft. It is roughly 12.5 miles round trip to Upper Eagle Lake at 7,110 ft with only about 2,350 ft of gain, so it is a gentle carry by the standards of this range. Lower Eagle Lake at about 6,490 ft is the quieter option. Horsehead Pass at roughly 7,540 ft sits just above camp and is the gateway both to Boiling Lake on the far side and to the ridge walking that reaches Switchback. Linking on to Martin Lakes and Cooney Lake makes a longer circuit that takes in more of the southern summits. Season is roughly July into October; the pass holds snow on its north side later than the approach suggests. Be aware that Upper Eagle can be crowded and noisy on a fine weekend - if you want quiet, camp at Lower Eagle or push over the pass.
bivy.water: Both Eagle Lakes, and Eagle Creek is bridged on the way up. Above the lakes, on the pass and along the crest, there is nothing; carry water for any traverse day.
bivy.permit: Forest Service, no overnight permit needed. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the Eagle Lakes / Crater Creek trailhead. This trail is open to motorcycles and stock as well as walkers, which surprises people. Fires are restricted most summers and firewood at 7,000 ft is not a renewable resource here.
bivy.capacity: Many sites - almost every level spot around Upper Eagle Lake gets used, plus a large horse camp just below it and further sites at Lower Eagle Lake about a mile off the main trail. This is the busiest backcountry camping in the range.

wa_switchback_mountain_scramble.notes: A higher start at about 4,760 ft and a gentler grade, with a creek ford. From the Crater Creek trailhead follow the Eagle Lakes trail a little over two miles, then the Martin Creek trail to the Cooney Lake trail; parties can also base at Upper Eagle Lake and cross Horsehead Pass. Often used to make a loop with the Foggy Dew side.
hazards: Creek ford on the Crater Creek and Eagle Lakes side
Lightning exposure on an open ridge and summit with nowhere to shelter
Loose rock and talus on the southeast ridge
Dry ground above the lakes; no water on the pass or crest
Off-trail route-finding from the pass to the summit
Snow lingers on the north side of Horsehead Pass later than the approach suggests
Trail shared with motorcycles and stock

wa_the_brothers_south_couloir.name: Lena Lake and the Brothers climbers' path (summer)
wa_the_brothers_south_couloir.notes:
Lena Lake Trailhead (Trail #810) off FS-25, around 700 ft. About 3 miles and 1,100 ft of gain on maintained trail through second- and old-growth, crossing several creek drainages, to Lena Lake at roughly 1,800 ft — a busy backpacking destination with a ranger station, and the last easy reliable water and camping before the climbers' route.

Skirt the west side of the lake and pick up the unmaintained but well-trodden Brothers boot path, which follows the East Fork Lena Creek drainage through the old-growth known as the Valley of the Silent Men for roughly 2.5-3 miles to a climbers' camp around 2,900 ft, marked by a fire ring. Most parties use this as high camp for a two-day ascent.

Route-finding gets hardest immediately after leaving camp for the summit push, where the boot path repeatedly appears to vanish. Follow a climbers' path upstream and west along the west fork for about a mile. It crosses an avalanche debris field where slide alder and downed logs — some with hand-lines or steps cut into them — hide the line, and creek fords may be needed. Beyond the debris field the path re-enters forest and climbs toward the couloir.

Water is reliable at the lake and up Lena Creek to high camp. Above camp there is nothing dependable once you are on scree and snow.
wa_the_brothers_south_couloir.season: Jun-Sep; by late August the couloir is often scrambling rather than snow
hazards: avalanche debris field of slide alder and downed logs between high camp and the couloir, with possible creek fords
moat opening at the base of the Hourglass as the snow recedes
thin snow bridge through the Hourglass constriction in spring
misleading cairns on the upper route
class 4 with real exposure on the last 200 ft
no reliable water above high camp
wa_the_brothers_south_couloir.baseFinding:
You are at the base of the actual climb when the climbers' path fades out in a large meandering gully at the bottom of a broad debris and deposition fan, with the couloir narrowing above it — roughly 4,000-4,300 ft. The path ending is the marker; there is no cairn or sign.

Above that, two features tell you the route is going right.

The Hourglass, near 5,800 ft, is a narrow rock and snow constriction and the crux of getting to the summit block: a couple of exposed 3rd-to-4th class moves in summer, or a steep 35-45 degree snow neck in spring which can be a thin snow bridge and which opens a moat at its base as it melts.

Higher, at the top of the snow, there is a notch with a large rock in it. Climb around that rock to the right to reach the scree gully beyond. The general rule reported by parties who lose the thread here is: when in doubt, go right.

Cairns exist most of the way, but several of them are misleading. Treat a cairn as a hint and the terrain as the authority. The final roughly 200 vertical feet to the true south summit is class 4 with real exposure.

wa_the_brothers_south_couloir.name: Early-season snow ascent
wa_the_brothers_south_couloir.notes:
The classic time for this route is early season, roughly April into May, because the gullies fill in with dense brush later and the snow-covered version is much faster.

The approach is the same — Lena Lake, the Brothers boot path up the East Fork, the climbers' camp near 2,900 ft — but the avalanche debris field between camp and the couloir is easier under snow, and the couloir itself becomes a snow climb requiring an axe and reliable self-arrest rather than a scree slog.

Snow also buries the boot path, so the route-finding difficulty immediately above camp is worse, not better: there is no tread to find at all.
hazards: avalanche hazard in the couloir and on the approach slopes
thin or collapsing snow bridge at the Hourglass
steep 35-45 degree snow requiring axe and solid self-arrest
no boot path visible under snow above high camp
wa_the_brothers_south_couloir.baseFinding:
The deposition fan at the foot of the couloir is still the mark, but under snow the fan and the couloir merge visually. Read it by width: the base is where the open fan narrows into a defined couloir line, several hundred feet of which you then climb before exiting onto its west side and continuing up toward the spur.

The Hourglass around 5,800 ft is the feature to inspect from below. In spring it is a steep snow neck at 35-45 degrees and is sometimes a thin snow bridge — a moat at its base is the sign it is going.

The notch with the large rock at the top of the snow is still passed on the right.

wa_the_scoop_2.name: Colchuck Lake outlet into the west cirque
wa_the_scoop_2.notes:
Stuart Lake Trailhead (NF-7601 off Icicle Creek Road; Northwest Forest Pass). Stuart Lake Trail #1599 for roughly 2.25 miles with a Mountaineer Creek log bridge near 1.5 miles, to the junction where Colchuck Lake Trail #1599A branches left; a second Mountaineer Creek log crossing, then steepening rocky switchbacks to Colchuck Lake — about 4 miles and 2,280 ft, roughly one and three-quarter to two hours for a fit party.

The shorter line into the west basin: cross the lake's outlet below the small dam at the north end and follow the climbers' path up and across the timbered hillside straight into the cirque — about an hour from the lake, plus 15 to 25 minutes of boulder-hopping to the wall. Colchuck Lake is the last dependable water; carry what you need for a long day.
hazards: Slick or partly submerged log bridges over Mountaineer Creek early season
Loose talus in the basin and the final scramble
No water above Colchuck Lake
Snow lingering in the basin into early summer
wa_the_scoop_2.baseFinding: In the basin, The Scoop starts to the right of the West Face and the Tempest and to the left of Rikki Tikki Tavi. The confirmation is not at the ground but three pitches up: the first three pitches, to about 5.10a, lead to launch ledge, the platform sitting directly below the namesake Scoop corner. If the ledge you reach after three pitches has no large corner system rising above it, you are not on The Scoop. Expect loose 3rd/4th class rock in the final approach scramble to the wall.

wa_the_scoop_2.name: Aasgard-side lakeshore, slide alder, leftmost gully
wa_the_scoop_2.notes: Follow the lakeshore climbers' path counter-clockwise toward the Aasgard Pass slopes, gaining talus and heather about 400 ft above the lake, then cut north through the slide-alder band — cairned, but a genuine bushwhack of 15 to 20 minutes. Take the left-most gully and climb it about 1,000 ft to its top, then contour east on an easy path into the basin. One and a half to two hours from the lake, more gain than the outlet line but no ford.
wa_the_scoop_2.season: Jul-Sep; ice axe useful before mid-July
hazards: Wet snow on the Aasgard slope into July
Dense slide alder
Loose gully talus; late snow in the gully
wa_the_scoop_2.baseFinding: Cairns mark the base of the correct gully and stop there. Leftmost is the test. From the basin, The Scoop is right of the West Face and Tempest and left of Rikki Tikki Tavi; Launch Ledge, three pitches up with the Scoop corner above it, is what confirms the line.

wa_the_tooth_south_face.name: Snow Lake Trail to Great Scott Bowl and Pineapple Pass
wa_the_tooth_south_face.notes: Upper Alpental lot at the end of Alpental Road (about 3,100 ft), I-90 exit 52. Take the Snow Lake Trail (#1013) north; a cat track runs up the valley from the end of the lot, just left of the stream, before the tread narrows to normal trail. At roughly 1.5-1.6 miles a small signed junction splits Source Lake from Snow Lake — bear left toward Source Lake. Cross the Source Lake basin contouring near 4,000 ft, then at about 4,400 ft you crest a lip and drop into Great Scott Bowl (also called Pineapple Basin). Work up the bowl on talus, or on snow if any remains, toward Pineapple Pass at the head of it, passing beneath the Fang — the pinnacle on the bowl's west side that carries the Edge of Time route. The common error is here, not lower down: a boot path running around the back of the Fang leads into the gully between the Fang and the Tooth. Parties who take it have to backtrack several hundred feet through trees and rock fields to get back onto the right ground. The second error is going straight up to Pineapple Pass itself — that col is the rappel line down, not the way up.
hazards: loose talus underfoot the whole length of Great Scott Bowl
steep sustained snow slope below Pineapple Pass in early season - axe, sometimes crampons
moat, and in some years a cornice, where the bowl's snow meets rock at the pass
rockfall from parties above on a face that is often busy
no reliable water past the Source Lake outlet
wa_the_tooth_south_face.baseFinding:
From Great Scott Bowl, scramble to the notch just south of Pineapple Pass, then contour clockwise around the Tooth's south side. The last part of that contour is short class 3-4 and is not exposed; if it feels serious you are on the wrong ground.

You are at the start when you are standing under a broad, blocky face roughly 400 ft high with an obvious big vertical crack system splitting it. The first moves are easy ramps that angle left to a large rectangular block, then back right into that crack system. About 100 ft up, the first belay is a slung rock horn with a balanced, flat-topped block sitting on it — that block is the confirmation you are on the standard line.

Two negative markers. If you are looking up a steep, narrow gully rather than an open face, you are in the gully between the Fang and the Tooth, one formation short — go back down and continue around. And if you scrambled straight up into a notch with rappel slings hanging above you, you are standing at Pineapple Pass on the descent route; downclimb and take the next notch south, then contour.

In early season a steeper gully runs up toward the base of the face. Do not use it unless it is filled with snow.

wa_the_tooth_south_face.name: Winter and spring, snow-covered Alpental valley
wa_the_tooth_south_face.notes: Once there is meaningful snow the summer tread is not the route. The talus slopes the summer trail crosses are the Alpental valley's avalanche chutes — seventeen of them are counted along its length — and the winter line instead climbs the valley on the south side of the South Fork Snoqualmie toward Source Lake rather than following the summer switchbacks across those paths. From below Source Lake, traverse up into Great Scott Bowl, typically on an upward-traversing line on the west side of the bowl passing beneath the Fang, and join whatever track leads to Pineapple Pass. Most parties cache skis or snowshoes in the bowl before the final slope. The entire trip through the Source Lake and Snow Lake basins is avalanche terrain; this is a stability decision, not a route-finding one.
hazards: avalanche terrain the full length of the Alpental valley - roughly seventeen chutes cross the summer trail line
the summer boot path is not a safe winter line once snow is present
cornices at Pineapple Pass
moat between the snow and the rock at the top of the bowl
creek crossings near the Source Lake outlet at high early-season flow
wa_the_tooth_south_face.baseFinding:
The finish is the same: the notch just south of Pineapple Pass, then a clockwise contour. Under snow the thing that decides where you can actually reach rock is the moat at the top of the bowl's snow. Probe it, and be ready to work around its edge on rock rather than force the direct step across.

With the base buried, the start, where easy ramps lead left to a large rectangular block, can be under snow. If you cannot find that block, you are probably below the true start — keep contouring around rather than climbing the first weakness above you, which is what puts parties into the gully between the Fang and the Tooth.

wa_three_fingers_south_peak_lookout.name: Tupso Pass trailhead, Trail #641 (road drivable)
wa_three_fingers_south_peak_lookout.notes:
Trail #641 from the Tupso Pass trailhead at the end of FR 41. Forest to Saddle Lake at about two and a half miles — the last easy water, with no fires and no camping within two hundred feet of the shore beyond this point — then up through meadows to Goat Flats at roughly four and a half miles, which has the best camping on the route and views out to Puget Sound.

From Goat Flats the trail climbs about two more miles to Tin Can Gap at roughly six miles, banking most of the day's gain. That is the effective end of the maintained trail and where most walkers turn back.

The trail has been maintained by volunteers in recent years, with large numbers of logs cleared; note that a big fallen log above Saddle Lake has rerouted the tread, and there is a rough connector going straight up and down to the next switchback.
hazards: moat between glacier and rock that widens through the season and is hard to enter in poor visibility
crevasses on the Queest-Alb once it opens up
exposure on the ladders, particularly between the second and third
unverified fixed hand-line on the rock step past Tin Can Gap
wa_three_fingers_south_peak_lookout.whyThisWay: Only if the Forest Service repairs the Canyon Creek bridge and reopens FR 41 to Tupso Pass: then it is a long day or an easy overnight instead of a 31-mile trip.
wa_three_fingers_south_peak_lookout.baseFinding:
Past Tin Can Gap you drop off-trail onto the Queest-Alb Glacier. Late in the season you can avoid the ice entirely by staying in the moat between the top edge of the glacier and the rock — and finding the entrance to that moat is the thing that goes wrong in bad weather. The trail crosses back to the north side of the ridge shortly before it and you meet the top of the glacier there; if you are on the south side of the ridge you have not crossed over yet.

The start of the actual climbing is not in doubt once you can see it: three wooden ladders, stacked in sequence and pinned into the rock with rebar and steel cable, run up the final rock band to the lookout deck. There is nothing else like them on the mountain. The transition between the second and third ladder is the hardest move and is awkward with a full pack, and the exposure is real.

The negative marker is which summit you are on. The lookout — and therefore the ladders — is on the south peak. If you have crossed the glacier and are scrambling rock toward a col with no ladders anywhere in view, you are heading for the Middle or North peak instead. Some parties also report a hand-line on a short exposed rock step just past Tin Can Gap before the glacier; treat any fixed rope there as unverified.

wa_three_fingers_south_peak_lookout.name: Road-closure variation — walk or bike FR 41
wa_three_fingers_south_peak_lookout.notes:
FR 41 is closed to vehicles at the washed-out Canyon Creek bridge, leaving roughly nine miles of road between the closure and the trailhead. Vehicles are barred past the barrier but foot and bike traffic are allowed, and biking the road is the common tactic.

Treat this as a standing possibility rather than a one-off: check with the Darrington Ranger District or the Verlot Public Service Center before committing, because the difference is a day hike versus an overnight. There is now a sign at the road marking the old trailhead.
hazards: several miles of road walking or biking each way with the resulting late finish
all the hazards of the standard variation once on trail
wa_three_fingers_south_peak_lookout.baseFinding: Once you reach Tupso Pass the route is identical, and the same markers apply: cross to the north side of the ridge past Tin Can Gap to meet the top of the Queest-Alb, find the moat entrance rather than stepping onto open ice, and finish on the three stacked ladders on the south peak.

wa_thunder_mountain_north_face.name: Surprise Creek past Surprise and Glacier lakes
wa_thunder_mountain_north_face.notes: The more popular way in, from a trailhead that is easy to find near Scenic on US 2. Climb the Surprise Creek trail to Surprise Lake, join the Pacific Crest Trail and follow it north to Trap Pass, then take the unofficial path south from the pass to the Thunder Mountain lakes basin under the north face.
hazards: Rarely repeated 600 ft class 5 line, first climbed 1972; rock quality and protection unconfirmed
Loose or lichen-covered alpine granite likely on an infrequently climbed face
Unofficial, unmarked path south of Trap Pass to the lakes basin under the face
Remote setting with sparse modern beta

wa_thunder_mountain_north_face.name: Tunnel Creek, Hope Lake and the PCT

bivy.name: Trap Lake
bivy.notes: The closest camp to Slippery Slab Tower and the best base for Thunder Mountain. Two trailheads reach it: Tunnel Creek, which climbs about a mile and a half to Hope Lake on the Pacific Crest Trail and then runs south a couple of miles over meadowy ground before the switchbacks up to Trap Pass; or Surprise Creek at Scenic, which climbs to Surprise Lake and joins the Pacific Crest Trail heading north. Trap Lake sits a little below Trap Pass on the east side. From the pass a faint but obvious climbers' track branches south along the ridge crest, follows it to a boulder field, and works up that to the base of the tower — the whole point of camping here rather than at the Scenic lakes is that it puts a party at the pass within half an hour of leaving the tent. Slippery Slab Tower is a single pitch of pleasant lower fifth class on an arete whose flakes are not to be trusted for protection, so it is a short climb with a long walk attached, and an overnight makes the arithmetic work. Thunder Mountain itself is a scramble from the same ground. The Thunder Mountain Lakes further south are a delicate basin where camping is discouraged; use this lake instead. Season is roughly July to October, with snow on the Trap Pass switchbacks well into summer.
bivy.water: The lake, and the inlet above it. Treat it.
bivy.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness. A free self-issue permit is required for day and overnight use, taken at the trailhead register from mid-May to the end of October. A Northwest Forest Pass is required at the Surprise Creek trailhead. Campfires are prohibited above 4,000 feet west of the crest, and a stove is the right answer here in any case.
bivy.capacity: Several small informal sites in the trees at the lake, below the pass on the east side of the crest. Quiet, and rarely more than a party or two.

bivy.name: Thunder Mountain Lakes
bivy.notes: Lake basin under the granite of Slippery Slab Tower and Thunder Mountain, reached by the unofficial trail south from Trap Pass. The closest camp to the north face. Fragile ground; camp only on rock or bare sites.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit
bivy.capacity: A few small sites on durable ground

wa_thunder_mountain_north_face.notes: From the Tunnel Creek trailhead off US 2, climb about a mile and a half to Hope Lake on the Pacific Crest Trail. Follow the PCT south a couple of miles over meadowy ground and up the switchbacks to Trap Pass, then take the unofficial path south to the Thunder Mountain lakes basin.
hazards: Snow on the Trap Pass switchbacks well into summer
Rarely repeated 600 ft class 5 line, first climbed 1972; rock quality and protection unconfirmed
Loose or lichen-covered alpine granite likely on an infrequently climbed face
Unofficial path south of Trap Pass to the lakes basin; fragile ground at the lakes
Remote setting with sparse modern beta

wa_trapper_mountain_south_slopes.name: Up the valley from the landing, then off-trail into the lake basin
wa_trapper_mountain_south_slopes.notes:
There is no road to this side of the peak. Reach the valley by ferry or floatplane, then take the valley road or the park shuttle to a campground and pick up the valley trail from there. The lake below the peak is reached by leaving that trail and pushing off-trail and unmarked into the basin - a steep, poorly marked fisherman's path at best, and map-and-compass travel above it. Figure a full day of travel each way and plan on two or three days with a camp at or below the lake.

The off-trail departure is not well defined; plan it from current maps and imagery before you go.
wa_trapper_mountain_south_slopes.season: Midsummer through early autumn, once the basin is walkable and the valley road and trail are open
hazards: reaching the valley at all depends on a ferry or floatplane and a shuttle
an unmarked off-trail push into the basin with no reliable path
loose unconsolidated talus and steep heather benches with unstable footing
no tread to follow on the descent, on ground where every slope looks the same
an exposed class 3 finish off the ridge
conflicting records of the approach drainage, so the departure point must be planned from maps
wa_trapper_mountain_south_slopes.baseFinding:
The lake is the anchor and the route is read from it. The lake sits immediately north-east of the summit, so from the water the peak is to the south-west.

Leave the lake basin and gain the broad basin and slopes on the peak's south side, aiming for the low point on the summit ridge rather than for the summit itself. There are no cairns and no path here; the terrain is the navigation.

The ground confirms itself as you gain height: loose unconsolidated talus interspersed with heather benches on a steep grade, with unstable footing and no established tread. Note your ascent line, because on the descent one talus-and-heather slope looks exactly like the next and there is nothing to follow.

The finish is the test that you chose the right side. From the ridge the last stretch to the top is a short exposed class 3 scramble. If the ground above you is a steep continuous snow line splitting the summit block, you have come round onto the north side and are under the couloir route, which is a different proposition entirely and wants an axe, crampons and a season this route does not.

Also confirm the peak: a similarly named summit elsewhere in the range is approached from a completely different valley. The lake immediately north-east of your summit is what identifies this one.

wa_trapper_mountain_south_slopes.name: Over the pass at the head of the river road and down to the lake from the west
wa_trapper_mountain_south_slopes.notes:
The lake can also be reached from the other side of the range, by climbing to the pass at about 5,392 ft at the head of the river road - or the nearby col used when the pass is corniced - and then travelling east, descending and traversing through the basin beyond to the lake at about 4,170 ft.

This avoids the ferry and the unmarked valley push entirely, at the cost of a pass crossing in each direction and a descent that has to be re-climbed at the end of the trip.
wa_trapper_mountain_south_slopes.season: Late spring into summer, while the pass is straightforward and the basin beyond is still simple travel
hazards: a corniced pass in early season
a descent from the pass that must be re-climbed on the way out
loose talus and heather with unstable footing and no tread
an exposed class 3 finish
a basin with no path and no obvious exit seen from above
wa_trapper_mountain_south_slopes.baseFinding:
From the pass the travel is east and downhill to the lake, so the arrival marker is water at about 4,170 ft with the peak standing to the south-west of it.

From the lake, the south slopes are gained by going round the peak, not up the side facing you. The face you can see from the lake is the northern one. The route is on the opposite flank - the broad basin and slopes above the lake basin on the south side, taken toward the low point on the summit ridge.

The negative marker is the snow line. If you are looking up at a continuous couloir splitting the summit block and are tempted by it, that is the north couloir route and not this one. It is a snow climb with a different season and different equipment.

The positive markers on the route are underfoot: loose talus and heather benches on a steep grade, with no cairns, followed by an exposed class 3 scramble off the ridge to the top. Note your ascent line for the descent, because nothing here is marked.

wa_upper_north_ridge_w_great_gendarme.name: Goat Pass and the Stuart Glacier to the fourth-class gully and the notch
camps: Upper Ingalls Creek meadows, below Stuart Pass
Ingalls Creek basin camp, below Longs Pass
wa_upper_north_ridge_w_great_gendarme.notes:
From the Esmeralda Basin trailhead at the end of the North Fork Teanaway Road, take the Ingalls Way trail over Ingalls Pass, past Ingalls Lake toward Stuart Pass, then the climbers' path onto the talus shoulder under Stuart's West Ridge and northwest to Goat Pass at about 7,600 ft.

From Goat Pass, traverse onto and across the Stuart Glacier rather than along beneath it, aiming for a fourth-class gully that runs up to the obvious notch in the North Ridge. This is the difference between this route and the complete ridge in one sentence: the complete-ridge party traverses east below the glacier to the toe, this party crosses the glacier and goes up.

The notch is a bivy: there are two good sites in it, which is why parties who intend to climb the upper ridge in a day from a high camp use it.

Published descriptions of this route are frank that the last of the navigation is yours — one of them says outright to take a topographic map and work it out. Treat that as a real warning rather than as rhetoric.
wa_upper_north_ridge_w_great_gendarme.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; earlier the gully to the notch holds snow and the glacier crossing is simpler, later it is bare and looser
hazards: Crevasses on the Stuart Glacier crossing from Goat Pass
Loose rock in the fourth-class gully to the notch, with parties above
Knife-edge exposure on the ridge above the notch
Gendarme bypass gully is rockfall-prone on dirty rock and not recommended
Upper mountain is shaded and cold, icy on the crux pitches
Awkward retreat from the Gendarme's offwidth; navigation above the notch is on you
wa_upper_north_ridge_w_great_gendarme.baseFinding:
The notch is a place you can sit down, and that is the test. There are two good bivy sites in it. If you have arrived somewhere on the crest with no flat ground, you are not at the notch — you have gained the ridge somewhere else along its length.

The approach to it is a fourth-class gully off the Stuart Glacier, not a scramble up the ridge flank. If the ground you are climbing is open face rather than a defined gully, you are not in the right line.

Orientation at the notch, which settles it: standing in the notch, the whole lower ridge falls away below you to the north and the Ice Cliff Glacier is on the far side of it. Everything above you is the upper ridge, and the Great Gendarme is roughly eight or nine pitches up from here. If the big tower is already below you, you have joined the crest above the notch and above two of the route's three named features.

What you have deliberately given up: about 1,200 ft of climbing, including the sustained lieback crack that is the hardest pitch on the complete ridge. So the notch is not a shortcut to be found by accident — a party that meant to climb the complete ridge and ends up here has walked past its own route. Confirm which climb you are on before you start up.

wa_upper_north_ridge_w_great_gendarme.name: Mountaineer Creek and the Stuart Glacier from the north

bivy.name: North Ridge notch bivy
bivy.notes: The ridge is gained at roughly 8,200 ft from the upper Stuart Glacier at about 7,800 ft via a snow-filled gully usually climbed on fourth-class rock along its edge, and the notch just above is the last genuinely comfortable bivy before the climbing proper. A second cluster of usable ledges sits several pitches higher, above the junction with the lower west variation, which suits parties splitting the Complete North Ridge over two days. Everything here is an emergency-grade perch rather than a campsite: no water, no shelter, and no easy retreat once committed. Whether to bivy at all is a live disagreement — many parties climb the route in a single push from Goat Pass, and which is better depends on your speed and the descent you have chosen.
bivy.water: None on the ridge. Fill from snowmelt streams on the traverse below the Stuart Glacier before committing, or melt snow from the glacier; there is nothing above.
bivy.permit: No separate climbing permit exists for the ridge itself, and the wilderness permit requirement is driven by which drainage you camped in. Parties staging from Ingalls and the Esmeralda side need only the free self-issued Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit; parties who camped in Mountaineer Creek below are in the Stuart Zone and need that overnight permit May 15 to Oct 31. The boundary in the upper basin is not clearly drawn — confirm with the Wenatchee River Ranger District if you intend to bivy low on the north side.
bivy.capacity: Around four or five people at the notch itself, with a scattering of poorer spots higher on the ridge; the good ledges are few and far between once you are on the route

wa_upper_north_ridge_w_great_gendarme.notes: From the Stuart Lake trailhead, follow the trail up Mountaineer Creek, then leave it for the climbers' path into the basin below the Stuart and Sherpa glaciers. Climb the Stuart Glacier to the notch where the upper ridge begins. This suits parties camping in the north-side basin, but leaves the car on the opposite side from the Cascadian Couloir descent.
hazards: Stuart Glacier climbed to reach the notch; crevasse hazard on the glacier
Snow-filled gully to the ridge, usually climbed on fourth-class rock along its edge
Off-trail climbers' path from Mountaineer Creek into the basin below the Stuart and Sherpa glaciers
Knife-edge exposure on the ridge above the notch
Gendarme bypass gully is rockfall-prone on dirty rock and not recommended
Upper mountain is shaded and cold, icy on the crux pitches
No water on the ridge; bivy ledges are few and exposed
